name: Suspicious npm preinstall hook — pipe to shell
description: package.json preinstall script pipes network fetch to shell execution (curl|wget|fetch piped to sh/bash). This is the primary Miasma/Shai-Hulud infection vector.

name: Suspicious npm postinstall hook — pipe to shell
description: package.json postinstall script pipes network fetch to shell execution.

name: npm lifecycle script — inline node eval
description: Lifecycle script uses node -e to execute inline JavaScript. Common obfuscation technique for droppers.

name: npm lifecycle script — bash -c execution
description: Lifecycle script spawns a shell via bash -c or sh -c. Used to execute encoded/obfuscated payloads.

name: npm lifecycle script — base64 decode
description: Lifecycle script contains base64 decoding. Indicates payload obfuscation typical of Miasma variants.

name: Phantom Gyp — command substitution in binding.gyp
description: binding.gyp contains command substitution via <!(). This bypasses npm script monitoring and executes arbitrary code via node-gyp during install.

name: Phantom Gyp — node execution in binding.gyp
description: binding.gyp executes node with inline eval or script. May be legitimate (nan, node-addon-api) — check allowlist.

name: IDE config injection — Cursor AI rules in repo
description: The repository contains Cursor AI rule files. If injected by an attacker, these can instruct the AI assistant to introduce vulnerabilities into future code.

name: IDE config injection — Claude AI settings in repo
description: The repository contains Claude AI configuration files. These can be poisoned to alter AI coding assistant behavior.

name: IDE config injection — VS Code tasks in repo
description: The repository contains a VS Code tasks.json that can execute arbitrary commands when the project is opened.

name: IDE config injection — VS Code tasks with shell command
description: VS Code tasks.json contains shell execution. If committed by an attacker, this auto-executes when a developer opens the workspace.

name: CI/CD injection — GitHub Actions workflow with curl pipe
description: GitHub Actions workflow contains a run step that pipes a network fetch to shell. Classic exfiltration or dropper pattern.

name: CI/CD injection — GitHub Actions secret exfiltration
description: GitHub Actions workflow appears to exfiltrate secrets or environment variables via network requests.

name: CI/CD injection — GitHub Actions base64 decode in run
description: GitHub Actions run step contains base64 decoding, indicating obfuscated payload execution in CI.

name: Git hook injection — executable hooks committed to repo
description: Executable git hooks are committed in the repository tree. If not from a known hook manager (husky, lefthook), this may indicate persistence.

name: Python setup.py — cmdclass override with shell exec
description: setup.py overrides build/install commands with shell execution. Used in PyPI supply chain attacks to execute code during pip install.

name: Python setup.py — network fetch during install
description: setup.py imports urllib/requests at module level and makes network requests. Code execution during pip install should not require network access.

name: Python setup.py — base64 or exec obfuscation
description: setup.py contains base64 decoding or exec/eval of encoded strings. Strong indicator of obfuscated malware dropper.

name: Env exfiltration — inline script accesses environment secrets
description: An inline script (node -e, python -c, or shell) accesses environment variables commonly containing secrets (AWS keys, tokens, SSH keys).

name: Suspicious .npmrc — registry override
description: .npmrc sets a custom registry URL. If unexpected, this could redirect package downloads to a malicious mirror.

name: Suspicious .npmrc — token committed to repo
description: .npmrc contains an embedded authentication token. This is a credential leak that enables package hijacking.

name: Suspicious .pypirc — token committed to repo
description: .pypirc contains embedded PyPI credentials. This enables package hijacking via credential theft.
